body:
The central comparison

Geographical indications, plant variety protection and trade secrets all recognise valuable interests, but they differ in subject matter, legal conditions and the conduct they can restrict. The correct answer in a preliminary examination often depends on identifying what is protected, who holds the relevant right and what exception applies.

FeatureGeographical indicationPlant varietyTrade secret
Protected subjectQualifying goods linked to geographical originEligible plant varietyGenuinely confidential commercial information
Indian frameworkGI Act, 1999PPV&FR Act, 2001Contracts and breach-of-confidence principles
RegistrationRequired for statutory registered-GI infringement rightsRequired for registered variety rightsNot required
Key rightsAuthorised users may use the GI; proprietor and users can enforce itBreeder and other entitled persons have specified commercial rightsHolder may act against unlawful disclosure or misuse
Important limitationGoods must satisfy origin and registration conditionsFarmers' and researchers' exemptions applyIndependent discovery and lawful reverse engineering remain possible
Duration10 years, renewableStatutory periods vary by categoryDepends on continued secrecy and other legal requirements
Transfer or licensingRegistered GI rights generally cannot be assigned or licensedBreeders may authorise agents or licensees as provided by lawConfidential know-how can be shared or licensed under appropriate agreements

Applying the distinctions to common situations

Situation 1: A regional textile is copied elsewhere

If a registered Gujarat GI identifies a particular textile associated with a defined region, the legal issue is whether the copied goods are being presented with that registered geographical indication in an infringing manner. Making a visually similar textile does not, by itself, establish geographical origin. The GI protection concerns the registered indication and the statutory conditions surrounding its use.

Situation 2: A farmer saves seed from a protected variety

If a farmer retains seed from a harvested protected variety for the next sowing, section 39's farmer exemption is directly relevant. If the same person instead packages and markets branded seed of the protected variety, that activity cannot simply be justified by citing the farm-saved seed exemption.

Situation 3: Two businesses independently develop the same method

If one business keeps a method confidential but another develops it independently without wrongdoing, the first business generally cannot use trade secret law to prohibit the independent method. A trade secret claim is concerned with unlawful acquisition, use or disclosure of qualifying confidential information, not every instance of another person possessing the same knowledge.

Situation 4: A researcher uses a protected plant variety

Experimental use of a registered variety and its use as an initial source for developing another variety are protected under section 30. Repeated use of the protected variety as a parental line when necessary for commercial production of the newly developed variety, however, requires the registered breeder's authorisation.

One-glance decision framework

When distinguishing these systems, avoid relying only on whether the subject is commercially useful. Geographical origin must be linked to the goods; a variety must satisfy the applicable registration criteria; and information claimed as a trade secret must remain genuinely confidential.

Prelims focus

  • 1999: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act.
  • 2001: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act.
  • 10 years: Basic renewable GI registration period.
  • NDUS: Novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity and stability for a new plant variety.
  • Section 39: Important farmers' rights, including the exception concerning branded seed.
  • Trap: Trade secret protection cannot ordinarily prevent lawful independent discovery merely because someone else held the same knowledge confidentially.

[Sources: Intellectual Property India, Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, sections 2, 17–24; India Code, Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001, sections 15, 24, 28, 30 and 39; WIPO, Trade Secrets, sections on qualifying information and limits of protection, consulted 14 November 2026; WIPO, Overview of National and Regional Trade Secret Systems: India, sections 1–4, June 2024.]
